item.title: Snoop Dogg wants to pay you $10K a month to taste ice cream all over the world
item.description: In a video posted to his social channels on Aug. 27, Calvin Broadus Jr., the rapper known more widely as Snoop Dogg, announced the search, saying “I’m hiring an international ice cream taster at Dr.
item.dc:creator: Sydney Wray
item.content:encoded: There is a new job on the market: International Ice Cream Taster. And the hiring manager? Iconic American rapper and entrepreneur Snoop Dogg. In a video posted to his social channels on Aug. 27, Calvin Broadus Jr., the rapper known more widely as Snoop Dogg, announced the search, saying “I’m hiring an international ice cream taster at Dr. Bombay.” Snoop Dogg’s ice cream company, Dr. Bombay, which he launched in partnership with his son in 2023, has partnered with HR company Deel to hire someone who can “chill worldwide.” Are you qualified? Well, according to Snoop, you just need a valid passport and to be “detail-oriented.” The posting also says that you can be located anywhere in the world. The one-of-a-kind job is fully remote and pays a whopping $10,000 per month. It is unclear what currency that figure is in, though Dr. Bombay’s headquarters is in Los Angeles. “We need help finding new flavours,” says the video posted to Snoop Dogg’s socials. According to Deel’s website, “This isn’t a publicity stunt dressed up as a job posting - it’s a real position with real compensation ($10K a month).” The online job application has applicants share links to their social channels as well as answer questions such as: More than 200,000 people have applied worldwide, according to social posts from Deel and Dr. Bombay. Posts across platforms show applicant-made creative videos explaining why they are the ideal candidate for the role. Deel has reposted several creators’ videos pitching themselves for the job via all kinds of methods from raps to actual taste test auditions. The link to apply has been posted to LinkedIn and other social platforms for worldwide applicants to take their shot.

item.title: Bank of Canada holds key rate at 2.25% as tariffs, Iran war cloud outlook
item.description: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada is set to make its sixth interest rate decision of the year this morning. Most economists and financial markets favour another rate hold from the central bank today.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Canada held its benchmark interest rate steady again on Wednesday as new U.S. tariffs and the ongoing war in Iran cloud the central bank’s outlook. The Bank of Canada’s policy rate remains at 2.25 per cent after a seventh straight hold. The move was widely expected by economists. Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said Wednesday that the persistence of the Middle East conflict has increased inflationary risks as global energy prices continue to float higher. A new tariff battle with the United States meanwhile threatens Canada’s burgeoning economic rebound, he said. That renewed uncertainty might lead businesses to delay investment and hiring decisions until the trade picture crystallizes. Because the economy was evolving broadly in line with the bank’s forecasts, governing council opted to keep the policy rate unchanged on Wednesday, Macklem said. “Monetary policy cannot offset the effects of tariffs or influence global energy prices. What we can do is ensure global developments don’t jeopardize price stability in Canada,” he said. Monetary policymakers at the Bank of Canada use the policy rate to keep a lid on inflation and support economic growth when prices are contained. Macklem was tight-lipped in a press conference with reporters after the decision about whether the bank is more concerned about inflation or growth risks in the midst of an uncertain outlook. “The risks are shifting and we are prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed,” he said. Inflation was a full percentage point above the Bank of Canada’s two per cent target at three per cent in July. The Iran war drove a volatile period for gas prices over the spring and summer. Macklem said that’s too high for the bank’s comfort. He said its rate decisions are still guided by its inflation forecast, which will be updated at the next rate announcement on Oct. 28. Economic growth, meanwhile, has shown signs of rebounding after stagnating for much of the last year. The economy surged with 3.3 per cent annualized growth in the second quarter, though few analysts expect that same pace continued into the current quarter. The spectre of a re-escalating trade war with the United States loomed over the Bank of Canada’s decision Wednesday. The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods on Aug. 22 and has threatened steeper duties on autos. Macklem said the central bank doesn’t expect a “large direct impact” on the economy from the newest tariffs, though targeted sectors could be hit hard. He said he expects growth in the fourth quarter will take a hit from the new duties. Canada is planning a slate of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods starting Sept. 8. Macklem said the inflationary risks from Canada’s counter-tariffs are “fairly modest” and that the global energy shock remains the biggest tailwind to higher prices. Before the latest U.S. tariffs came into effect, exports were starting to rise again. While Macklem warned that new trade restrictions could see business confidence hampered again, he also expressed some optimism about firms’ ability to cope with an uncertain status quo. “Businesses have been adapting to an environment with more uncertainty, higher tariffs … they’re finding ways to do business,” Macklem said. “That has put the Canadian economy on a better footing going into this latest new wave of U.S. tariffs,” he said. Macklem also reiterated that most of the things that will insulate the economy from tariff threats — like diversifying Canadian exports to new markets — are not in the Bank of Canada’s purview. Much of that work needs to be done by governments and the private sector, he said. Some economists weighing in after the rate decision Wednesday argued that Macklem’s focus on rising inflationary risks in his statement gives the Bank of Canada a bias toward rate hikes, rather than cuts. Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the central bank will likely need to see further signs of improvement in the unemployment rate or economic growth before raising the policy rate. But given that global oil prices have shown little signs of easing, he said a rate hike at the bank’s final meeting of the year in December is now on the table. KPMG chief economist Ali Jaffery said in a note that he expects the bank to be less worried about inflation given the sharp risks for lower growth in the face of escalating tariffs. His call remains for the Bank of Canada to stay on hold through the end of 2027. CIBC chief economist Avery Shenfeld said it was no surprise the central bank left its key rate unchanged “amidst the fog of a trade war.” Shenfeld said CIBC sees “little prospect” for any change in the policy rate this year, given that both the U.S. tariff and Iran war fronts could shift in the months ahead. Financial markets had three quarter-point hikes baked into their forecasts by mid-2027 as of Wednesday at noon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. Odds of a hold at the Bank of Canada’s next decision in October stood at more than 94 per cent. --- Craig Lord, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

item.title: Auto sales see third consecutive month of gains in August: DesRosiers
item.description: DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc. says auto sales in August were up 5.4 per cent, marking the third consecutive month of sales gains.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: RICHMOND HILL — DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc. says auto sales in August were up 5.4 per cent from a year ago, marking the third consecutive month of sales gains. The firm estimates 168,000 vehicles were sold in the month, up from 160,000 in August 2025. Andrew King, managing partner at DesRosiers, says the market was still a ways off the highs seen during the 2017 to 2019 period, when August sales consistently topped 180,000 units. But he says last month’s sales were still a solid performance, given the geopolitical tensions and trade dispute between Canada and the United States. Looking ahead, DesRosiers says this month’s auto sales could come in lower, compared with September 2025. An escalating tariff war and the ongoing affordability crisis could weigh on auto sales as households rein in spending. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.
